item.description:
This live blog is now closed. You can read our latest full report here:

  • Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say

Some more Gulf reaction to Houthi’s deadly airport attack and continued threats to target Saudi airspace.

In a significant message, the United Arab Emirates has issued a statement in solidarity with Saudi Arabia – expressing support for “all measures aimed at safeguarding the kingdom’s security and stability”.

The UAE message is improtant given the major rupture in relations this year between the two oil-rich kingdoms, first sparked by lingering divisions in Yemen, and made worse by the Iran War and arguments over oil prices which led to the UAE quitting OPEC (currently led by the Saudis) after six decades of membership.

Saturday’s incident comes amid an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis ⁠on the kingdom. The airport has already been attacked twice this ​week, leaving four people dead and ‌others wounded, and ‌badly damaging an aircraft.

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Chin up, Zack! It was never going to be plain sailing for the new-look Greens
item.description:
Chin up, Zack! It was never going to be plain sailing for the new-look Greens

Submitted by Tom Blackburn on Sat, 10/10/2026 - 13:40
The party should not allow the Holborn and St Pancras by-election to become a referendum for its entire project; its convictions have altered the political landscape for the better
Green Party leader Zack Polanski pictured following the results in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, triggered by the resignation of former PM Keir Starmer as MP for the constituency, London, UK, 9 October (Reuters/Toby Shepheard)
Off

In the end, for all the sound and fury, Labour held Holborn and St Pancras with relative ease. Sagal Abdi-Wali’s majority of just under 3,400 was down from Sir Keir Starmer’s 11,000 margin at the last general election in 2024, but on a substantially lower turnout of 38 percent. 

The Green Party in England and Wales’ hopes of making a major breakthrough in another Labour heartland, as with Gorton and Denton in February, were dashed on this occasion.

No doubt the result will come as something of a disappointment for the Greens, and for their leader and by-election candidate Zack Polanski. However, the Labour Party has held the constituency ever since its creation in 1983 and, with Starmer gone and Andy Burnham still enjoying something of a honeymoon period, winning in Holborn and St Pancras was always a lot to ask of the Greens, although they did manage to increase their share of the vote by 22.3 percent.

Even if this is something of a setback in the near term, the Greens’ showing in Holborn and St Pancras isn’t necessarily a verdict on their longer-term prospects. But with some of the party’s old guard visibly uncomfortable with its left-populist direction under Polanski and now making their discontent increasingly public, the party faces a choice between panicking and retreating, or holding firm and building on its very real recent gains.

What is clear is that Burnham’s rise to the leadership of Labour, and the premiership, has changed the political calculations considerably. Burnham is a far more capable and skilled politician than Starmer ever was; much more personable, better able to read changes in the political winds and adjust to them.

Starmer, meanwhile, is now free to do what he probably always wanted: flatter his way into the top job at Nato, where he can deal solely with other elites and not have to bother with the little people.

Altering course

Owen Jones, among others, has argued that the Greens can already take much of the credit for changing the political landscape, and for making Labour change direction. Not only was Starmer forced out, but Burnham himself has felt it necessary to make some policy and rhetorical concessions to the left. 

It is still early days for Burnham, and many voters remain prepared to give him the benefit of the doubt. Compared to Starmer’s intransigence and inflexibility, even modest concessions can look more significant than they really are.

The Greens made headway under Polanski precisely because the party has offered a more radical, outspoken alternative to Labour

However, this should not be confused with any fundamental alteration in Labour’s political orientation. The Greens would do well to remember that a Labour bounce was always likely, but also that such bounces are usually only temporary.

The fact that the Labour Party has enjoyed a modest revival under Burnham does not mean that the underlying grievances people held against it have vanished.

Predictably, the mainstream media have seized on the result in Holborn and St Pancras to push a crisis narrative, to imply that Polanski’s leadership of the Greens might be under threat and to frame the by-election result as a personal repudiation of him. Polanski is beginning to receive the Jeremy Corbyn treatment: his legitimacy continually questioned, every issue personalised regardless of the particular circumstances.

Caroline Lucas, who cuts an increasingly embittered figure, provided further ammunition in her appearance on Newsnight on Thursday night, shortly after polls had closed. When asked whether Polanski should resign, Lucas pointedly refused to defend him.

She then stepped up her attacks in a subsequent New Statesman article, arguing that the Zionism is Racism motion passed at the party’s conference last weekend “crosses a very significant red line”.

Lucas bemoans the fact that the motion “effectively denies Israel’s right to exist”, insisting that “Zionism is not a clearly defined, singular ideology”, but one that “means different things to different people, whether we like it or not”. These abstract theoretical distinctions, however, are worthless. In the real world, Zionism’s actual track record is one of ethnic cleansing, racism and genocide from the Nakba in 1948 to the present day. The burden is not on Palestinians or their supporters to sugarcoat it.

Some of the Green Party’s old guard, including Lucas, mutter darkly about “entryism” - as did the Labour right under Corbyn. But the party’s shift to the left is the product of a legitimate groundswell, not a clandestine takeover.

Polanski, of course, won the Greens’ leadership election last year with a colossal 84.1 percent of the vote. His support within the party remains very strong and, at present, there are no obvious rivals for the leadership. Anyone who attempted to challenge Polanski from his right would likely be humiliated.

The risk for the Greens is that they interpret every disappointment or hostile headline as evidence that they need to tone things down. But the party has made headway under Polanski precisely because it has offered a more radical, outspoken alternative to Labour, and it has, to an extent, forced Labour to steal its clothes. Retreating from this position back to a more innocuous, left-liberal stance would only take the Greens back to the margins.

As good as it gets

Furthermore, this is about as good as things are likely to get for Burnham. The structural conditions that fuelled the Greens’ earlier rise remain. A new analysis from the Joseph Rowntree Foundation warns that this Labour government is set to preside over the worst parliament for living standards in modern times, with average household incomes forecast to be lower in 2029-30 than when the party assumed office two years ago.

What’s shameful is that no party before the Greens called Zionism racist
Read More »

Burnham has insisted that he will not call an early general election before 2029. But Gordon Brown lived to regret not doing the same when he had the chance in 2007: a reminder that the political outlook can easily turn on a dime, and that no new prime minister is guaranteed a lasting honeymoon.

The Greens should therefore not allow the Holborn and St Pancras by-election to become a referendum on their entire project. They have time to develop their policies on living standards, including housing and public services, and to build a firmer presence in communities beyond their existing strongholds.

The Green Party has come a long way in a short space of time, but it was never going to be entirely plain sailing. It can emerge from this relatively minor setback more confident and better prepared for the next opening.

But the party must also learn to be steadfast against the growing media hostility it faces; it should articulate its position on Palestine clearly and consistently, resisting the temptation to flap whenever opponents and internal critics invoke one supposed red line or another.

It should ignore the siren song of the media and the political establishment, and reject any cynical efforts to hype up a single by-election defeat into a mandate for ditching entire planks of either its domestic or foreign policy.

The Houthi attacks over the weekend marked a sharp escalation in the Yemen war.

On Sunday, a strike hit Riyadh's international airport, killing one person, just hours after another Houthi-claimed attack on the site killed 13 people and left hundreds of others wounded, forcing authorities to suspend operations there

Speaking at a conference in Riyadh, the country's Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said the attacks, the deadliest to have hit the kingdom in a decade, have "tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience. They have also tested decisions made long before present crises, because resilience is built before crises begin".

"Energy security can't be taken for granted," he added.

"The events of recent weeks are serious, our response must be equally serious."

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] UK advises against using any Saudi airport except Medina
item.description:
UK advises against using any Saudi airport except Medina

Submitted by Imran Mulla on Mon, 10/12/2026 - 09:12
The UK has further warned British nationals not to try and leave Saudi Arabia via airports in the country
An air traffic control tower is seen at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on 19 September 2026 (AFP)
Off

The British government has advised its citizens against all but essential travel to parts of Saudi Arabia, including Jeddah and Dammam, and to all airports in the country except Medina International Airport. 

The UK has further warned British nationals not to try and leave Saudi Arabia via airports in the country.

This comes after a fresh attack on a passenger terminal at Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, which killed at least one person and wounded 11.

Saturday's attack on the airport killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 - making it the deadliest strike on a Gulf country since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on 28 February.

Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement that four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed in the attack. 

It was the third attack on the airport in a week, following earlier strikes that killed four people and damaged a Saudi commercial aircraft.

The British Foreign Office updated its official guidance on Sunday to advise UK nationals against "all but essential travel to all airports within Saudi Arabia except for Medina International Airport", as well as "all but essential travel to Aseer province, Riyadh province, Najran province, Jizan province and the cities of Taif, Jeddah and Dammam".

Houthi forces warn against use of Saudi airports following Riyadh attack
Read More »

The Foreign Office further advised against all travel to within 10km of the border with Yemen.

"As an alternative to airports within Saudi Arabia," the Foreign Office said British nationals wishing to depart Saudi Arabia should consider options to travel by land to neighbouring countries and fly from there.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree warned travellers, airlines and shipping companies not to use Saudi airports and airspace, saying they are “exposed to targeting and a theatre for operations by our forces”, with the exception of the airports of Mecca and Medina.

Saree said Houthi forces carried out several operations against King Khalid airport on Saturday, “resulting in the disruption of air traffic at the airport and its complete closure”.

He also listed King Fahd Airport in Dammam, an Aramco-affiliated petrol station and a refinery in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Region among the targets.

'Dangerous escalation'

The latest attacks mark a significant escalation in the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi movement in Yemen, with renewed fighting and a Saudi-led military offensive against the group. 

British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting condemned Saturday's airport attack as a "dangerous escalation" and "completely contemptible action".

Meanwhile in Yemen, air strikes have been reported on the Hamdan district in Sanaa and two more strikes on al-Zurbi Road in the Hayfan district in Taiz, according to Sanaa-based media. 

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan activate Mecca Pact amid war with Houthis

Missile attacks were also reported on the border district of al-Dhaher in Saada province. No casualties have been reported so far. 

The US State Department has urged American citizens to take "extreme caution" when travelling through airports in Saudi Arabia, amid renewed attacks.

"U.S. government employees working in Saudi Arabia require special authorization to use the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, as well as the airports in Jeddah and Dammam," its official account on X said.

"Please take extreme caution when using all major airports in Saudi Arabia. U.S. citizens should be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions."

Amid the escalation, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spoke over the phone to his Saudi counterpart Faisal bin Farhan.

According to Iranian state media, Araghchi said Iran was ready to help start dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen. 

He expressed concern over escalating tensions, and insisted that a "military approach and ignoring a political solution will further complicate the current situation".

Araghchi also further stressed that crisis in the region "have no military solution", adding that Tehran is "ready to provide any assistance to help start dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen and to help achieve a political solution".
